positions/wider-hope-accessibilism/oneLi: Salvation is only through Christ, but God may save those who never heard the gospel if they respond in faith to the light they receive, or by encountering Christ at or after death.
positions/wider-hope-accessibilism/coreC: Christ is the only saviour (ontological necessity) but explicit knowledge of him may not be required (epistemological openness).
God desires all to be saved (1 Tim 2:4) and judges according to the light people have (Rom 2:6–16).
Old Testament and pagan believers (Abel, Enoch, Job, Melchizedek) were saved by faith without knowing Jesus.
Some propose that the unevangelised meet Christ after death (1 Pet 3:19; 4:6).
positions/wider-hope-accessibilism/origi: Anticipated by Justin and Zwingli (who hoped to meet Socrates in heaven), John Wesley, C. S. Lewis (The Last Battle, 1956) and Norman Anderson; argued by Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God’s Mercy, 1992) and John Sanders (No Other Name, 1992); post-mortem versions by George Lindbeck and Gabriel Fackre.
positions/wider-hope-accessibilism/stron: It holds together Christ’s uniqueness and God’s universal saving will.
Scripture includes believers outside Israel who knew God without the Law or Christ.
It avoids the apparent arbitrariness of restrictivism without embracing pluralism.
Restrictivists argue it undermines the urgency of mission and contradicts Romans 10.
There is no clear biblical example of someone saved through another religion after Christ came (Cornelius still needed Peter).
Pluralists see it as a half-way house that still privileges Christianity.
positions/wider-hope-accessibilism/respo: Advocates answer that mission brings the fullness of salvation, assurance and the Church, not merely escape from hell.
They claim no certainty about how many are saved, only hope grounded in God’s character.
positions/wider-hope-accessibilism/conse: A significant minority view among evangelicals and Wesleyans.
Controversy in the Evangelical Theological Society in the 1990s (open theism debates with Pinnock and Sanders).
positions/inclusivism-anonymous-christia: Inclusivism ("anonymous Christians")
Rahnerian inclusivism
Fulfilment theology of religions
Catholic inclusivism

Christ is the unique saviour of all, but his grace is at work beyond the visible Church, including in and through other religions, so that sincere non-Christians may be saved by Christ without knowing him explicitly.
God’s universal saving will (1 Tim 2:4) means grace is offered to every human being.
Other religions may contain "seeds of the Word" and "rays of truth" and mediate grace in a provisional way.
All who are saved are saved by Christ and ordered toward the Church.
Dialogue and mission are both necessary: dialogue respects truth in others; mission makes explicit what is anonymous.

Roots in Justin’s Logos theology and the fulfilment theology of J. N. Farquhar (The Crown of Hinduism, 1913); formulated by Karl Rahner (1961) and taught in Lumen Gentium 16 and Nostra Aetate (1964–65); developed by John Paul II (Assisi prayer meetings, 1986; Redemptoris Missio, 1990) and Jacques Dupuis.

It integrates the scriptural witness to Christ’s uniqueness with texts about God’s universal light.
It recognises the evident goodness and holiness in many adherents of other faiths.
It has become official Catholic teaching through an ecumenical council.
Particularists argue it weakens the necessity of explicit faith and of mission.
Pluralists and adherents of other faiths find "anonymous Christian" patronising, as if a Buddhist were a Christian without knowing it.
Critics ask why, if other religions mediate grace, the Church is needed at all.
Rahner answered that the label is a Christian self-description of hope, not a claim imposed on others.
Catholic teaching (Redemptoris Missio, Dominus Iesus) insists that dialogue does not replace mission and that the Church remains the ordinary means of salvation.
Vatican II teaching on salvation and the religions.
Formal interreligious dialogue (Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue, 1964; Assisi 1986).
Debates over Jacques Dupuis and Asian Catholic theologies.
positions/religious-pluralism/oneLine: The major world religions are equally valid, culturally conditioned responses to one ultimate divine Reality, and none, including Christianity, is uniquely true or uniquely saving.
positions/religious-pluralism/coreClaims: The Real (God) lies beyond all human concepts; religions are different human responses to it.
Salvation is the transformation from self-centredness to Reality-centredness, visible in many traditions.
Incarnation language is mythological or metaphorical rather than literal (Hick).
Dialogue and cooperation for justice should replace conversion (Knitter).
positions/religious-pluralism/origin: Precedents in Enlightenment deism, Lessing’s Nathan the Wise (1779), Ernst Troeltsch and Wilfred Cantwell Smith; formulated by John Hick (God and the Universe of Faiths, 1973; An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) and The Myth of Christian Uniqueness (Hick and Knitter, 1987); Asian voices include Stanley Samartha and Raimon Panikkar.
positions/religious-pluralism/strongestA: Religious belief correlates strongly with birthplace, which seems to make exclusive truth claims arbitrary.
Saintliness and moral transformation appear across religions.
It fosters peace and respect in religiously plural societies.
positions/religious-pluralism/strongestO: Most Christians judge it incompatible with the New Testament’s witness to Christ’s uniqueness and with the creeds.
Critics (Newbigin, D’Costa) argue it is itself an exclusivist, Western-Kantian position that redefines all religions in its own terms.
Adherents of other religions often reject the claim that their faith is "one path" to the same Reality.
positions/religious-pluralism/responses/: Pluralists reply that every theory has a vantage point, but theirs is more inclusive and humble.
They argue that Christian commitment can be wholehearted without being exclusive ("love language" of devotion).
positions/religious-pluralism/consequenc: Influence in liberal Protestant seminaries and interfaith organisations.
Catholic disciplinary responses (Dominus Iesus, 2000; notifications on Dupuis and others).
positions/religious-liberty/name: Religious liberty as a Christian principle
positions/religious-liberty/oneLine: Because faith must be free and every person bears God’s image, no one may be coerced in religion by the state or others; the church proclaims by persuasion, and states should protect freedom of religion for all.
positions/religious-liberty/coreClaims/0: Genuine faith cannot be compelled (Tertullian: it is not part of religion to compel religion).
positions/religious-liberty/coreClaims/1: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world; its weapons are spiritual (John 18:36; 2 Cor 10:4).
positions/religious-liberty/coreClaims/2: Religious freedom is grounded in human dignity and the nature of faith (Dignitatis Humanae).
positions/religious-liberty/coreClaims/3: Freedom includes worship, teaching, changing one’s religion and corporate church life.
positions/religious-liberty/origin: Early apologists (Tertullian, Lactantius) pleaded for freedom; after Constantine and Augustine’s acceptance of coercion against Donatists it faded. Anabaptists (Hubmaier, On Heretics and Those Who Burn Them, 1524), Baptists (Thomas Helwys, 1612; Roger Williams, 1644), Quakers (William Penn) and Enlightenment thinkers revived it; the Catholic Church embraced it in Dignitatis Humanae (1965) and the WCC in 1948.
positions/religious-liberty/strongestArg: Coerced faith is not faith; Jesus never forced belief.
Centuries of religious wars and persecutions show the evil of coercion, including by Christians against Christians.
It protects Christians themselves, who are today among the most persecuted religious groups.
positions/religious-liberty/strongestObj: Before 1965 much Catholic teaching (e.g. Pius IX’s Syllabus of Errors, 1864) held that error has no rights and the state should favour the true religion.
Traditionalists argue Dignitatis Humanae contradicts earlier magisterial teaching.
Some argue that unlimited liberty enables proselytism and social fragmentation, a concern voiced in some Orthodox and Muslim-majority contexts.
positions/religious-liberty/responses/0: Defenders answer that development of doctrine, rooted in human dignity and the freedom of the act of faith, explains the change (Murray, Ratzinger).
positions/religious-liberty/responses/1: They distinguish legitimate witness from coercive or manipulative proselytism.
positions/religious-liberty/consequences: Catholic support for democracy and human rights after 1965.
Christian advocacy for persecuted minorities worldwide.
Constitutional protections such as the US First Amendment and Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948).
positions/liberal-protestantism/oneLine: Christian faith must be reinterpreted in the light of modern knowledge (historical criticism, science, philosophy), locating its essence in religious experience and the ethical teaching of Jesus rather than in dogma or an infallible text.
positions/liberal-protestantism/coreClai: Religion is grounded in experience (Schleiermacher’s feeling of absolute dependence) or moral value (Ritschl), not in authoritative propositions.
The Bible is a human record of revelation, to be studied with the same historical-critical methods as other texts.
Doctrines are historically conditioned expressions of faith that can and should be restated.
The heart of the gospel is the fatherhood of God, the infinite value of the human soul and the ethic of love (Harnack).
God works immanently through history, evolution and human progress.
positions/liberal-protestantism/origin: Rooted in the Enlightenment and Romanticism, it was founded as a theological movement by Friedrich Schleiermacher (On Religion, 1799; The Christian Faith, 1821–22), developed by Albrecht Ritschl and Adolf von Harnack in Germany, Horace Bushnell and the Social Gospel in America, and by Catholic Modernists (Alfred Loisy, George Tyrrell) until condemned by Pius X (1907). 20th-century heirs include Rudolf Bultmann’s demythologising (1941), Paul Tillich and process and progressive theologies.
positions/liberal-protestantism/stronges: It takes honest intellectual inquiry seriously and refuses to set faith against established historical and scientific knowledge.
It makes Christianity intelligible and credible to educated modern people, as earlier theologians did for Platonists and Aristotelians.
It recovers the ethical, this-worldly emphasis of Jesus and the prophets, fuelling social reform.
It recognises the human, historical character of Scripture and doctrine, which the Bible itself displays.
Machen and other critics argue it is "a totally diverse type of religious belief" that keeps Christian words while abandoning the redemptive supernatural faith.
Karl Barth argued that grounding theology in human experience made God a projection of human culture, as shown by liberal theologians’ support for the German war in 1914.

Its optimism about progress was shattered by the World Wars; H. Richard Niebuhr caricatured it as preaching "a God without wrath" bringing "men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross."
Sociologically, liberal denominations have declined steeply in membership since the 1960s.
positions/liberal-protestantism/response: Liberals reply that the "essence" of Christianity has always been reinterpreted and that rigid orthodoxy, not liberalism, drives modern people away.
Post-liberal and progressive heirs have accepted many criticisms of naive progressivism while maintaining critical engagement with Scripture and science.
Membership decline reflects many factors (birth rates, secularisation) rather than theology alone.
positions/liberal-protestantism/conseque: Dominated leading Protestant universities and seminaries in Europe and North America by 1900.
Provoked the fundamentalist reaction and Catholic anti-Modernism, and later Barth’s neo-orthodoxy.
Shaped mainline Protestant churches, the Social Gospel and the ecumenical movement.
Historical-critical methods it championed became standard in academic biblical studies across traditions.
